claims.text: A non-fusion-deposited HEA coating will restore high-temperature wear resistance to the damaged component.
A non-fusion-deposited HEA coating will restore the component's mechanical integrity.
The coating repair will avoid the hot cracking associated with traditional fusion-welding repair.
The component material is sensitive to weld-induced microstructural changes and is prone to fusion-zone hot cracking.
CrCoFeMoNi with VC is a candidate HEA coating material for this intervention.
Cold spray or low-heat-input laser cladding can minimize heat input and avoid melting-related defects.
The deposited HEA will form a uniform wear-resistant surface layer.
The repaired region will have a stable microstructure and a minimal heat-affected zone.
A uniform coating and minimal heat-affected zone will bypass cracking pathways caused by conventional fusion processing.
Non-fusion deposition eliminates the high thermal gradients and rapid cooling cycles inherent in fusion welding.
Eliminating fusion-welding thermal gradients and cooling cycles prevents hot cracking.
CrCoFeMoNi + VC has a homogeneous microstructure containing vanadium-carbide-rich precipitates.
Vanadium-carbide precipitates enhance the coating's hardness.
The HEA microstructure and carbide precipitates enhance high-temperature wear resistance and microstructural stability.
The HEA-coated repair will produce fewer or no hot cracks compared with traditional fusion-welded repair.
The HEA-coated repair will provide equivalent or better high-temperature wear resistance than traditional fusion-welded repair.
Traditional fusion-welding repair often causes hot cracking and an undesirable heat-affected zone that compromises wear and structural performance.
The intervention is expected to remain effective under typical high-temperature, high-wear service conditions.
Long-term coating adhesion and behavior under extreme thermal cycling remain unvalidated.
Scalability of the non-fusion coating process to complex geometries is uncertain.

contradictions.description: Laser cladding is presented as an example of non-fusion deposition that avoids melting and eliminates fusion-like thermal gradients, but laser cladding ordinarily involves localized melting and thermal cycling; the proposed alternatives therefore do not share the stated mechanism.
The hypothesis specifies a non-fusion process, while the intervention leaves the process ambiguous between cold spray and laser cladding, which differ fundamentally in whether melting occurs.
